This is indeed viable, but its downside is that numerical Tokens, though flexible, aren't intuitively understandable for purpose and function, and excessive flexibility may lead to unlimited expansion. Relatively, semantic Tokens have limited flexibility but effectively converge design language, maintain structural clarity and consistency, and make systems more stable and manageable for long-term maintenance.

54.heading:
Slot Composition:
Component Extension Method
54.subtitle: Designing components is like assembling building blocks. When designing components, we inevitably encounter variants with similar functions. At this point, think about 'assembly principles'—through Slots and composition, replacing or adding blocks without changing component cores, letting the same component extend into different functions, states, and purposes. This expands large component capabilities through small component combinations, reducing repetitive design and development costs.

content.paragraph1: This topic was actually shared before. Recently Figma also demonstrated thinking about component design with 'slot-based composition': treating components as assemblable building blocks, letting the same component develop new uses and purposes in different scenarios. When we encounter similar functional requirements in design, sometimes there's a new component that seems similar to an old one—that's when we can think about 'assembly principles.' Using Slots and composition, replacing or adding blocks without changing the core, letting the same component extend into different functions, states, and purposes.
content.paragraph2: Taking the card in the illustration as example: the card reserves a Slot, allowing dates, icons, or photos to be inserted as needed. By replacing sub-components, you can expand the card's capabilities, corresponding to multiple scenarios without adding different variants. This not only converges design components but also reduces engineering time costs—because this process is more like stacking blocks rather than developing a new component from scratch.
content.paragraph3: So when designing components, the key is maintaining imagination and creativity, leveraging existing component combinations, letting old components expand new value in new scenarios. The goal of design systems is convergence and consistency, not endless expansion.

55.heading:
Token Inheritance Practice:
Fill-in-the-Blank Table Method
55.subtitle: When first learning Design Tokens, it's often unclear what inheritance relationships exist between various Tokens. At this point, make a simple comparison table, dividing Tokens into three columns: Reference Token, System Token, Component Token. Then pick a component like Modal, break it down into Card, Heading, Description, Button... sub-components, and fill in the Tokens each part uses into the table. This method helps clarify Token inheritance relationships and serves as practice to deepen understanding of Design Token structure.

content.paragraph1: For newcomers to design systems, Design Token is often the confusing part. Especially Token inheritance: how to design reasonably? How to plan so different components can share? When planning design system courses, one assignment has students do 'fill-in-the-blank exercises.'
content.paragraph2: One assignment has a table with columns divided into: Reference Token, System Token, Component Token—three roles to fill in. Then, pick a larger component from the project, like Modal, break it down into sub-components: Card, Heading, Description, Button, etc. Then use fill-in-the-blank method to fill in Tokens each part needs into corresponding columns. Through this practice, you can more intuitively understand Token inheritance relationships and better understand how to plan Tokens as foundations shareable across different components—especially helpful for Design Token beginners.
content.paragraph3: If interested, you can use the table below for fill-in-the-blank practice. After completion, feel free to share your answers in the comments—I'll check if they're reasonable and give some suggestions 😃

56.heading:
Typography Styles:
Planning and Convergence
56.subtitle: When planning design system typography, first organize 'commonly used text content' and clearly label their purposes and functions. This gives direction when establishing typography rules, avoiding accidentally creating many similar-looking text styles. A simple approach: design a complete article interface page, observe from actual screens what needs headings, body text, notes, etc., then organize and categorize these common styles, giving each its role and function.

content.paragraph1: When planning text styles in design systems, first list 'commonly used text' like: headings, subheadings, body text, notes, links, etc., then briefly label each text type's purpose and function. This gives direction when planning fonts and sizes, and avoids continuously expanding into many similar-looking styles without clear differences 😅
content.paragraph2: Additionally, we can first design a complete article layout page—because articles typically use more different text levels. From the article, organize needed styles one by one: where's the page main heading, section headings, regular body text, card titles, descriptions, links or notes, etc., then categorize by usage and explain purposes.
content.paragraph3: So typography planning should avoid being overly complex—especially when using fonts, best to keep within 2-3 types. This helps engineers manage font resources, saves project costs, and reduces development confusion. From my past company experience, our implemented text styles were under 10 types—actually quite sufficient throughout 😁 While text style choices can enrich visuals, also consider project complexity and learning curve, helping product teams reduce mixing similar styles.

57.heading:
Starting Early:
Design System Foundation
57.subtitle: Should you plan a design system in the early stages of a product? This is a question many people ask, and my answer is 'yes.' Especially during the startup phase—establishing your core design system and component library first can make future product iterations smoother, reduce communication costs, and improve development efficiency. If you don't have time or resources to build your own design system and component library, you can also leverage open-source component libraries as a foundation, which can still lay the groundwork for future systematization.

content.paragraph1: Many people are curious: do you need to plan a design system during the startup phase? My answer has always been 'yes.' The reason is simple: during the early stages, ideas and features change rapidly. To validate product direction, iterations are also very frequent. This rapid accumulation often unknowingly creates increasingly heavy technical debt.
content.paragraph2: This doesn't just happen at startups—many mature enterprises face the same problem. In the early days, the rush for speed often leads to skipping proper architectural standards and shared language. Later on, collaboration between designers and engineers becomes increasingly difficult. The larger the project scale, the higher the labor and time costs. When you finally want to start building a design system, you often need to invest even more time reorganizing and adjusting.
content.paragraph3: Therefore, even if you don't have time to build your own design system initially, you can choose a mature open-source component library as a foundation. These open-source component libraries are themselves complete design systems and can be branded and customized according to product needs, still laying a solid foundation for future systematization. This applies regardless of project size. Take my own example—when recently developing my studio's platform, I also started with the design system and component library, ensuring each component is tested and validated before being assembled into the product interface. When issues arise, I can immediately go back to the component library to make corrections. In this era, AI is perfect for helping produce 'parts' in component libraries, significantly improving development efficiency. Now is the best time to establish a systematic foundation :D

58.heading:
Design Tokens + AI:
Taming Vibe Coding
58.subtitle: I recently picked up some high-value insights at WebConf 2025 regarding Vue.js and AI collaboration—specifically about applying Design Tokens (Variables). We all dread that moment when AI hallucinates 'close enough' colors or weird spacing during development, right? Here's how we can train the AI to behave!

content.paragraph1: I recently picked up some high-value insights at WebConf 2025 regarding Vue.js and AI collaboration—specifically about applying Design Tokens (Variables). We all dread that moment when AI hallucinates 'close enough' colors like #FEFEFE or weird spacing like 17px during development, right? 😅 So how do we train the AI to behave?
content.paragraph2: 🎨 On the Design side: Once we define Variables in Figma, we use a plugin (like Variables Export) to generate a Tokens.css file. 🤖 On the Communication side: We feed this file to the AI (Cursor/VS Code) and set a strict Rule: 'Always prioritize checking these Tokens for development! If you can't find a matching style, ask me first. Never invent your own hex codes or raw numbers!'
content.paragraph3: By doing this, we embed our design context directly into the AI's 'brain.' Now, when we're in the flow of Vibe Coding, the resulting UI and components will adhere to our Design System as much as possible (let's say 90%—we still have to account for that 10% AI randomness XD). Say goodbye to those messy, 'wild' styles! 🫡

59.heading:
Vibe Coding:
Foundational Project Architecture
59.subtitle: The first step in starting Vibe Coding is understanding a suitable architecture for AI projects. By integrating frontend, backend, Storybook (component library), and Shared (common assets, logic, and standards) within the same workspace, we provide the AI with complete context~

content.paragraph1: The first step for Vibe Coding beginners is understanding a basic architecture suitable for AI development. A simple and complete project includes frontend, backend, Storybook (component library), and a Shared folder for common assets, logic, and standards, etc.
content.paragraph2: Why is structure so important? Integrating both frontend and backend code in one place allows the AI to more accurately understand the project's full scope, avoiding functional and logic integration difficulties caused by fragmented architectures. When we clearly define design standards and data logic in the Shared folder, the AI can automatically verify these standards before development, reducing messy redundant code and allowing components to be reused across the project.
content.paragraph3: While understanding these architectures might be challenging for beginners (it was for me too 😅), it's core knowledge if the goal is to develop a complete, 'viable product' with integrated frontend and backend. Once you master the project structure, you can direct the AI more precisely, for example: 'Please use the XX component from Storybook and place it on the right side of the main product's Header~'
content.paragraph4: Although Vibe Coding is highly efficient, if basic structural steps are skipped, the project may become increasingly difficult to maintain or direct in the later stages. By learning the fundamental program structure, we can collaborate with AI more simply, and our control over the product will grow day by day~

60.heading:

Design File Token Detection

content.paragraph1: The Figma Plugin: Token Linker mentioned last weekend has finally been approved 😃 This is a small tool developed with AI assistance last week. Let me formally introduce this tool and its features, hoping to help everyone solve the tedious work of organizing Design Tokens~ Token Linker 👉 https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1589120729239345070/token-linker

This tool can help us convert these values back to the configured Design Tokens. 61.heading:

Structured Token Naming

62.heading:
Design System:
The Moat in the Vibe Coding Era
62.subtitle: As Vibe Coding becomes widespread, design systems are more important than ever~ To avoid visual homogenization from AI-generated products, we can build our own design taste from visual elements to component assembly, creating products with unique identity in this era of 'fast output'!

content.paragraph1: As Vibe Coding becomes widespread, the barrier to product development has significantly lowered. However, due to similar prompts, product visuals are heading toward 'homogenization.' At this point, Design Systems are no longer just tools—they become the key moat for establishing differentiation.
content.paragraph2: To avoid products becoming AI-generated 'twins,' we can start from foundational design principles, derive unique visual elements and components, and then assemble them into products. Even though this takes a bit more time than directly generating styles, it can inject unique identity and taste into products.
content.paragraph3: I'm also an efficiency-focused product designer, but AI's value shouldn't be to skip design—it should help us accelerate building this system. In an era of quick results, standing out among many similar products ultimately depends on our understanding of product personality, not merely relying on similar style prompts. This is also one of the topics modern product designers need to think about: the conflict and balance between 'development speed' and 'brand value'~

63.heading: Help AI Think Through Context
63.subtitle: In the wave of Vibe Coding, we need to deconstruct products more meticulously: breaking down interfaces into components, then further extracting Design Tokens~ The more precisely these foundational elements and components are defined, and the clearer the structure, the better AI can grasp the logic of these 'building blocks' and more efficiently assemble complete products~

content.paragraph1: Vibe Coding without proper architecture leads to endless code bloat as features expand. As projects grow larger, later-stage management and maintenance become extremely difficult. This is very similar to teams that lacked 'design systems' in the past—without good standards and architectural constraints, product maintenance costs grow exponentially over time.
content.paragraph2:
So in the early stages of design and development, we can deeply deconstruct products:

Interface Componentization: Break down interfaces into independent Components

Element Standardization: Extract element settings from components as Design Tokens (colors, spacing, etc.)

Clear Definitions: Add clear purposes and naming logic to components and Tokens
content.paragraph3: Structured context allows AI to more precisely grasp how to use these 'building blocks' during development, reducing 'thinking and reasoning' time. AI won't blindly produce from scratch, but develops components through defined Tokens, then assembles components into complete products.
content.paragraph4: Although the initial investment is higher, it brings significant management advantages in the mid-to-late stages of product development. Building from small to large, having AI develop within standards effectively reduces duplicate code and chaotic component references, decreases AI's ineffective output, and accelerates overall development efficiency. This keeps the product in a controllable structure, rather than letting AI produce redundant, unnecessary, and messy code~
